title: Make a Wish

jokes.text: Norman building up 'good news' while Artie tries to cut through the theatrics
jokes.setup: Norman is milking the suspense of announcing good news as a publicist
jokes.punchline: Artie: 'Get on with it.' / 'Cause I'm wetting myself.' — Artie's aggressive impatience cutting through Norman's showbiz puffery
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie dry-dismissal comedy. The 'wetting myself' line is a deadpan deflation of Norman's excitement. Works because Artie's contempt for PR theatrics is baked into his character from episode one. Not exceptional but efficiently establishes tone.

dialogue.speaker: Publicist
dialogue.line: 'Cause I'm wetting myself.

jokes.text: 'You got us one that's not in a wheelchair this time, right?'
jokes.setup: The show has apparently done wish-foundation appearances before, framed as good PR
jokes.punchline: Larry's only concern about the sick child is whether the optics will be inconvenient for him — a casually monstrous non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: Extraordinarily character-specific. Only Larry Sanders — self-absorbed, image-obsessed, but capable of phrasing real awfulness in a breezy logistical tone — could deliver this line. The economy is perfect: one question, maximum darkness. The wheelchair detail makes it specific enough to be shocking rather than generic. Strong 7+ by any calibration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You got us one that's not in a wheelchair this time, right?

jokes.text: 'You wouldn't even know he's sick. It's something... ahem... internal.'
jokes.setup: Larry asked if the kid was in a wheelchair; Norman reassures him the kid is 'presentable'
jokes.punchline: Norman's qualifier — 'internal' — is meant to reassure Larry but inadvertently signals the child's condition is invisibly serious, making the reassurance absurd
jokes.explanation: A tight little joke about how Hollywood-minded people process illness entirely through optics. The 'internal' beat with its hesitation ('ahem') lands well because it reveals Norman's own discomfort even as he tries to manage Larry's.

dialogue.speaker: Publicist
dialogue.line: You wouldn't even know he's sick. It's something... ahem... internal.

jokes.text: Larry pivots immediately from the sick-kid good news to demanding to know about the 'Top 10 Sexiest Men Alive' list
jokes.setup: Norman has just revealed the People magazine opportunity around a dying child's wish
jokes.punchline: Larry's brain immediately jumps to what HE can get out of the People visit — the sexiest men list — exposing his narcissism with perfect timing
jokes.explanation: The pivot is perfectly timed — not a beat passes before Larry re-centers himself. Character-specific and structurally clean. The juxtaposition of charitable appearance and naked vanity is the DNA of Larry Sanders comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: Larry, as it turns out, you're number 11.

jokes.text: 'Larry, as it turns out, you're number 11.'
jokes.setup: Norman promised Larry he'd get him on People's Top 10 Sexiest Men Alive list
jokes.punchline: He didn't make it — number 11 — the cruelest possible near-miss
jokes.explanation: The specific number 11 is the whole joke — it's funnier than 'you didn't make it' because it implies Larry was SO close, making the failure more devastating. Economy is near-perfect: three words carry the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: Well, he's Batman, for Christ's sake.

jokes.text: 'Well, he's Batman, for Christ's sake... They could get Elmer fucking Fudd on that list.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks why George Clooney gets on the list; Norman explains the Warner Bros. publicity machine
jokes.punchline: The escalation from Clooney's Batman legitimacy to 'Elmer fucking Fudd' as the reductio ad absurdum of studio PR power
jokes.explanation: The Elmer Fudd escalation is genuinely funny — it's a perfect absurdist endpoint that also contains real industry commentary. 'Elmer fucking Fudd' is the right level of profane specificity. Quotable and surprisingly sharp for what's essentially a throwaway riff.

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: They could get elmer fucking fudd on that list.

jokes.text: Hank's entrance as 'Hank Kingsley, international cigar smuggler' doing a mock-Latino accent and announcing himself in Spanish
jokes.setup: The scene has been dealing with publicist anxiety and sick-kid stress
jokes.punchline: Hank bursts in performing a theatrical Spanish-smuggler persona, entirely oblivious to the room's mood — the comedy is his shameless self-mythologizing
jokes.explanation: Hank's theatrical self-importance is quintessential Tambor material. The 'international cigar smuggler' title is funny because of how seriously he wears it. The extended Spanish bit runs a beat too long for peak economy but serves to establish the cigar-smuggling plot engine.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hank Kingsley, international cigar smuggler.

jokes.text: Artie responds to Hank's Spanish cigar gifts with 'Ah, chinga tu madre. Hey! ¡chihuahua, pendejo!'
jokes.setup: Hank is performing his cigar-gifting ceremony with theatrical Spanish flair
jokes.punchline: Artie responds in equally fluent but profane Spanish, completely undercutting Hank's performance by out-authentically him
jokes.explanation: Artie knowing actual Spanish profanity and deploying it to puncture Hank's performance is very Artie — the world-weary veteran who always knows more than anyone gives him credit for. Short and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah, like in nuña your goddamn business.

jokes.text: 'Where do you get those, Hank?' / 'Oh, I get these from a guy named Nuña.' / 'Nuña?' / 'Yeah, like in nuña your goddamn business.'
jokes.setup: Larry sincerely asks where Hank gets the cigars
jokes.punchline: Hank delivers the 'Nuña / none of your' pun — an old schoolyard joke executed with Hank's particular brand of performative wit
jokes.explanation: The 'Nuña' pun is old — it's a playground joke — but Hank's delivery gives it slight character flavor since he's exactly the type to think this is clever. Low originality drags the craft score down. Gets a chuckle based on timing rather than wit.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: they put me between Dennis frantz and hector elizondo on the can you recognize these bald heads? Game.

jokes.text: 'You oughta keep that away from your crotch, or you'll end up on the dickless wonder list.'
jokes.setup: Hank is being warned about inhaling too much cigar smoke; Artie escalates the health warning
jokes.punchline: Artie's threat involves a cigar near the crotch resulting in castration, which he frames as an alternative list — a riff on the sexiest men alive conversation
jokes.explanation: Elegant mini-callback — 'dickless wonder list' mirrors the 'sexiest men alive list' and escalates the cigar danger into genital territory with Artie's signature deadpan. The callback makes it smarter than it would be as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You oughta keep that away from your crotch, or you'll end up on the dickless wonder list.

jokes.text: Artie's non-sequitur: 'I couldn't get Patrick Stewart on that thing.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks 'Were you the one on the left or right?' following Hank's bald-heads game story.
jokes.punchline: Artie casually drops that he tried — and failed — to get Patrick Stewart (famously bald, famously distinguished) onto the Sexiest Men Alive list, as if this is directly relevant.
jokes.explanation: Artie's deadpan insertion here is brilliant — it implies he's been quietly tracking this problem across multiple clients, it name-drops Patrick Stewart (genuinely sexy in his own right, which adds irony), and it arrives with zero fanfare. Pure Artie: maximum information, minimum words, perfect timing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You oughta keep that away from your crotch, or you'll end up on the dickless wonder list.

jokes.text: Artie explains why Charlie must be kept away from Larry: Larry cried uncontrollably during a show when Joan Embery brought in a baby fawn whose mother died in a brush fire — even while the Fly Girls were dancing
jokes.setup: Artie wants to protect Larry from emotional exposure to the sick child in front of the People reporter
jokes.punchline: The specific detail — 'even when the fly girls were dancing... he just kept blubbering about the fucking baby fawn's mother cooking in a brush fire' — reveals Larry's emotional volatility is both extreme and weirdly specific
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best bits of character writing. The comedy comes from stacked specificity: (1) it happened on air, (2) even the Fly Girls couldn't snap him out of it, (3) Artie characterizes the dead deer mother as 'cooking in a brush fire' with zero sentimentality, (4) it's so bad Artie calls it 'the worst show we ever had.' Each layer adds. The Fly Girls detail is the killer — it implies Larry was sobbing through a dance number, which is a vivid, absurd image. Very Larry Sanders: his emotions are real but catastrophically misplaced.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Larry couldn't stop crying even when the fly girls were dancing.

jokes.text: 'Maybe you should take your pants off and blow yourself.'
jokes.setup: Someone suggests she wear driving gloves to handle a cigar; she retaliates
jokes.punchline: A spectacularly profane non-sequitur comeback delivered as a casual suggestion
jokes.explanation: Shock value in the delivery and the casualness of the insult. Economy is good — it's direct and profane. But character integration is weak because the character delivering it isn't well-established in context. Gets a laugh from the audacity.

dialogue.line: He just kept blubbering about the fucking baby fawn's mother cooking in a brush fire.

jokes.text: The cigar-cutting havana room tangent: 'At the havana room, you know what they do? They cut your cigar for you. Those people, they know how to treat their celebrity clientele.'
jokes.setup: The group is fumbling with cigar paraphernalia.
jokes.punchline: Hank's wistful invocation of 'the havana room' — a place that treats him like the celebrity he considers himself — as a benchmark of civilization.
jokes.explanation: Competent Hank vanity joke but not particularly sharp. The 'celebrity clientele' self-designation is the only real sting. Passes but doesn't distinguish itself.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Maybe you should take your pants off and blow yourself.

jokes.text: 'What the fuck is that?' / 'It's a fan.' / 'What, is that, like, a gay thing?' / 'No, this is a gay thing.'
jokes.setup: Hank sees someone with a handheld fan and questions it
jokes.punchline: The response distinguishes between the fan (not gay) and whatever the person then does — 'no, this is a gay thing' — implying a physical demonstration that's funnier for being implied rather than stated
jokes.explanation: The misdirect is clean — you assume the comeback will define the fan as gay, but instead it points to something else entirely as 'a gay thing,' which is funnier for being unspecified. The exchange is well-structured and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What, is that, like, a gay thing?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: No, this is a gay thing.

jokes.text: The 'put the fan down / put the cigar down' standoff, followed by the '1, 2, 3' countdown where both immediately renege
jokes.setup: Hank and another person are locked in a petty standoff over cigar vs. fan
jokes.punchline: They agree to a simultaneous concession on the count of three, and the count immediately devolves — they both cheat, immediately breaking down the deal
jokes.explanation: Mild escalation comedy with a predictable structure (the 'on three' that fails), but the transcript suggests it derails fairly quickly. Functional filler rather than sharp writing.

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: I see vulnerability! 'Ben Stiller.'

jokes.text: Larry spots the People magazine sexiest list fax and immediately identifies Ben Stiller as the 'vulnerability' — the easiest to bump
jokes.setup: Norman offers to try to get a name bumped from the list to make room for Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately identifies 'Ben Stiller' as the softest target, then notes with irony that Ben is a friend who is on the show tonight
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Larry's complete lack of hesitation in identifying his 'friend' as expendable — and then the awareness that Ben is literally about to appear on the show adds dramatic irony that will pay off later. Good structural setup for future jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Just fucking bump him.

jokes.text: Norman counts to 10 to let Larry implicitly authorize bumping Ben without having to say it — Larry caves at '6': 'Just fucking bump him.'
jokes.setup: Larry can't bring himself to order his friend bumped from the list
jokes.punchline: Norman's passive-aggressive '1, 2, 3...' countdown forces Larry to crack — he can't maintain even 6 seconds of moral resistance
jokes.explanation: This is a gem. Norman's count-to-10 maneuver is a perfect piece of LA publicist psychology — he's giving Larry moral cover by making the betrayal passive. Larry's 'I can't... I can't... I can't say...' followed by snapping at '6' is exquisitely character-specific. It reveals everything about Larry: the thin ethical veneer, the self-awareness that it's wrong, and the complete inability to resist his own interests. The '4, 5, 6... just fucking bump him' timing is perfect. This is genuinely excellent sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: We don't have fucking time for this. 4, 5, 6... okay. Just fucking bump him.

jokes.text: 'Dean Cain, 3 boxes, Charlie Sheen, 2 boxes, Jason Priestley, 9 boxes.' / 'That kid's a chimney.'
jokes.setup: Norman reads out the cigar distribution list he's apparently been tracking
jokes.punchline: Jason Priestley ordered 9 boxes — prompting Hank's 'that kid's a chimney' with genuine admiration
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the celebrity names and quantities gives this texture — it's insider showbiz humor that feels real. The Priestley 9-boxes detail is the right punchline escalation, and 'that kid's a chimney' is an affectionate character note from Hank. Works because of specificity rather than novelty.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And if I didn't have a biscuit on me, it would've taken my arm off.

jokes.text: Hank's story about getting nervous at the airport: a drug dog 'lunged at him' — but 'if I didn't have a biscuit on me, it would've taken my arm off'
jokes.setup: Hank explains he's gotten nervous picking up cigars at the airport because of drug dogs
jokes.punchline: The dog didn't alert to contraband — it apparently just wanted the biscuit Hank happened to be carrying. The paranoid setup collapses into absurdist coincidence.
jokes.explanation: A nicely constructed small joke. The setup creates genuine tension (drug dogs, customs), then the punchline deflates it with an utterly mundane explanation (the dog was just hungry). 'If I didn't have a biscuit on me' is the right level of casual absurdity. Very Hank — he's oblivious to how funny his own story is.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, get a dick, will you?

jokes.text: Airport worker doesn't recognize Hank — thinks he was in Ghostbusters (Bill Murray) and Blues Brothers (John Belushi)
jokes.setup: Hank is at the airport and someone recognizes him as famous
jokes.punchline: They can't place him in anything he's actually been in — they keep guessing other actors. The only thing they remember is 'Canine' and even then they're more interested in the dog.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully character-specific. The running joke of Hank being barely recognized, then recognized for the wrong things, then upstaged by a dog ('that dog was cute') is perfect Hank Kingsley humiliation comedy. 'What's it like working with a dog?' / 'Pain in the ass' lands well — Hank's bitterness is equal parts self-awareness and obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Were you in ghost busters?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No. That was Bill Murray.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, how about blues brothers?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No. That was my brother John.

jokes.text: Beverly's reaction shot when she sees Charlie — 'Oh, my God.' — followed by a pause and 'I'm sorry'
jokes.setup: Beverly is introducing Charlie to the staff as if on a tour, maintaining cheerful professional composure
jokes.punchline: The involuntary 'Oh, my God' at seeing the child (clearly he looks ill) — immediately corrected by 'I'm sorry' — is a pure cringe beat of someone failing to hide their shock
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in implied visual comedy. The transcript shows us only 'Oh, my God.' [pause] 'I'm sorry.' — but the gap carries the whole joke. Beverly's professionalism collapses instantly on seeing Charlie, and the 'I'm sorry' tells us everything about what she saw. Economy score is very high because the joke is ENTIRELY in what's NOT said.

jokes.text: Phil doesn't realize Charlie is from the One Wish Foundation until told — then overcorrects with 'Oh, yeah, yeah! Hey, how's it going there?'
jokes.setup: Beverly introduces Charlie to Phil the writer; Phil initially thinks Charlie is Beverly's kid
jokes.punchline: Told Charlie is terminally ill, Phil's pivot to 'Oh, yeah, yeah! Hey, how's it going there?' — the aggressively casual tone of someone who has no idea how to handle this
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat. The cheerful 'how's it going there?' to a dying child is the comedy of someone trying too hard to seem unbothered. The rhythm of the awkward pivot is authentic to how people actually behave in this situation.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Beverly, I didn't know you had a kid.

jokes.text: Phil is asked to show Charlie how cue cards work: 'Oh, wow. You know? I wish I knew how to do that myself.'
jokes.setup: Beverly asks Phil to show Charlie how monologues are put on cue cards — presumably to keep the kid occupied
jokes.punchline: Phil, the head writer, admits he has no idea how the cue cards actually work — deflating both his own authority and the tour's educational value
jokes.explanation: A neat self-deprecating character beat. The writer admitting ignorance of the physical production of his own writing is both believable and funny. Economy is good — one line does the full work.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I wish I knew how to do that myself.

jokes.text: 'The kid creeps me out.' / 'It's really hard to be around someone who's ill.' / 'No, I don't give a shit about that. I just think it's weird someone's last wish is to meet Larry.'
jokes.setup: Two staff members are reacting to Charlie's presence
jokes.punchline: The staffer clarifies his discomfort — it's not the illness, it's the specific choice to spend a dying wish on meeting Larry Sanders that he finds inexplicable
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's darkest and most elegant joke. The misdirect is perfect: we expect the discomfort to be about illness, which would be the obvious (if uncomfortable) emotion. Instead, the line questions the value of Larry himself as a wish recipient — a quiet savage burn that cuts Larry, the show's premise, and celebrity culture simultaneously. 'I just think it's weird someone's last wish is to meet Larry' is devastating in its simplicity. High quotability, rewatch bonus for how much it rewards attention.

dialogue.line: I just think it's weird someone's last wish is to meet Larry.

jokes.text: 'Little Felipe needs a full moon to make the swim' — cigar smuggler explaining delayed delivery
jokes.setup: Hank's cigar source is explaining why the delivery is late
jokes.punchline: The explanation is theatrical and vague — 'full moon to make the swim' — which is either a smuggling metaphor or pure obfuscation, delivered with total seriousness
jokes.explanation: Nice bit of absurdist character texture from the cigar supplier. The poetry of 'little Felipe needs a full moon to make the swim' is genuinely funny in its unexpectedness — it's like a smuggler has convinced himself he's in a magical realist novel. Hank's 'that's bullshit, you know that's bullshit' grounds it.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: little felipe needs a full moon to make the swim.

jokes.text: 'I can't believe I actually introduced you to Dolph Lundgren.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just given the cigar supplier a lower-quality cigar as a substitute; the supplier accepts it, saying it'll get him 'all the way to my car'
jokes.punchline: Hank's parting shot — incredulous that he wasted a Dolph Lundgren introduction on this guy — implies his social currency is being squandered on an unreliable smuggler
jokes.explanation: A great Hank Kingsley joke because it reveals his currency: celebrity access. Dolph Lundgren as the specific name is perfect — not an A-lister, but exactly who Hank would know and brag about. The fact that an intro to Dolph Lundgren is his leverage in a cigar negotiation is both absurd and completely believable for Hank.

dialogue.line: This'll get me all the way to my car.

jokes.text: Mary Lou is standing near the parking space area, appears to be crying or emotionally compromised — Beverly's explanation: 'She has a lot of personal problems, sweetheart.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is trying to keep the tour upbeat; Mary Lou is visibly a mess
jokes.punchline: Beverly's breezy, matter-of-fact 'she has a lot of personal problems, sweetheart' — directed at the dying child — is a perfect piece of casual office dysfunction normalized
jokes.explanation: The delivery to Charlie — 'sweetheart' — while explaining an adult colleague's breakdown is the right absurdist register. Economy is high because one line captures the entire dysfunction of this office where everyone has personal crises and no one mentions it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Retooling?

dialogue.speaker: Jimmy
dialogue.line: Retooling.

jokes.text: The People reporter asks if Charlie has met Larry yet — he hasn't — she's surprised; Beverly pretends she was 'just taking Charlie to meet Larry'
jokes.setup: Beverly has been actively avoiding Larry for the entire episode; now the reporter is present
jokes.punchline: Charlie calls Beverly out in front of the reporter: 'I thought you said we were going on a yogurt run.' Beverly's cover story collapses in real time
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to the running stall gag. Charlie exposing Beverly's lie in front of the journalist is well-timed, and Beverly's scramble ('oh, no, baby, you got that all wrong') is classic sitcom damage control. The structure is clean: setup of the lie, arrival of the person who can't know, and the child blowing the cover.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Uh, she has a lot of personal problems, sweetheart.

jokes.text: 'Uncle Dennis Rodman's can of semen, just in case she wants another kid.' — Larry's desk piece joke
jokes.setup: Larry is rehearsing a comedy desk piece about Madonna's baby shower gifts
jokes.punchline: One of the 'gifts' is Dennis Rodman's preserved semen — a joke that ties into both Rodman's tabloid relationship with Madonna and its grotesque logistics
jokes.explanation: A period-specific topical joke (mid-90s Madonna/Rodman relationship). The 'in case she wants another kid' logic follows from the tabloid premise. Not particularly sophisticated but it's the kind of broad desk piece humor that works in context. Gets points for specificity and willingness to be crude.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I thought you said we were going on a yogurt run.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Oh, no, baby, you got that all wrong.

jokes.text: Larry mentions 'the Mommy's former lovers mobile' — a baby mobile with pictures of 1,000 different men
jokes.setup: Larry's baby shower piece continues with gift ideas for Madonna's newborn
jokes.punchline: The mobile concept — visual stimulation for infants via a parade of Madonna's lovers — is both functionally logical and aggressively vulgar
jokes.explanation: The joke's internal logic (babies need stimulation → this is stimulation) is its best feature. 'Mommy's former lovers mobile' as a compound noun is well-constructed. Period-specific celebrity humor but executed with reasonable craft.

dialogue.line: Uncle Dennis rodman's can of semen, just in case she wants another kid.

jokes.text: 'With the mobile comes the Sandra Bernhard swing, and it swings both ways.'
jokes.setup: Larry continues the baby shower gift riff
jokes.punchline: 'Swings both ways' — the double meaning (baby swing / bisexuality, in reference to Bernhard's known sexuality and her relationship with Madonna)
jokes.explanation: A clean double entendre with period-specific celebrity context. The wordplay is obvious but well-executed — 'swings both ways' is the right phrasing. Economy is high because one phrase does all the work. The joke is more TV-ready than truly clever.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So, uh... you got the Larry Sanders hat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Uh-huh.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's good.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What'd they charge you for that?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Why can't I get a Larry Sanders hat?

jokes.text: '...and with the mobile comes the Sandra Bernhard Swing, and it swings both ways.'
jokes.setup: Continuing the Madonna baby shower gift desk piece.
jokes.punchline: The Sandra Bernhard Swing 'swings both ways' — a double entendre on swing (baby equipment / sexual orientation), referencing Bernhard and Madonna's rumored bisexual relationship.
jokes.explanation: Clean wordplay with a topical hook. The 'swings both ways' pun is tidy and the celebrity reference is specific enough to work. Economy is strong — one phrase does double duty. Mid-tier late-night joke writing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Boy, how did you survive? This looks like hunter Thompson's pad in the sixties.

jokes.text: Larry asks Charlie what they charged him for the Larry Sanders hat — then asks why Larry himself can't get a Larry Sanders hat
jokes.setup: Charlie is wearing Larry Sanders branded merchandise
jokes.punchline: Larry — the person the hat is named after — doesn't have one, and is mildly annoyed about it. Larry is also confused about the economics of his own merchandise.
jokes.explanation: A perfect character joke. Larry's bafflement and mild grievance at not owning his own branded hat captures his particular brand of celebrity narcissism — he's simultaneously self-important (it's HIS hat) and strangely powerless. The question 'Why can't I get a Larry Sanders hat?' in the presence of a dying child who has one is a beautiful compression of everything wrong with Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Only you could make these goddamn sprinklers go off on some of the finest cigars in the world!

jokes.text: Beverly and Mary Lou defending themselves to Artie for letting the reporter catch them — Beverly's speech: 'we have covered every damn inch of this building and we ran out of ideas'
jokes.setup: Artie wanted Charlie kept away from Larry; Beverly and Mary Lou failed
jokes.punchline: Beverly's defense is total surrender — there were literally no more destinations left to stall with
jokes.explanation: A payoff line for the stalling subplot. 'We ran out of ideas' is honest and funny but not especially sharp. The scene works more as closure for the running gag than as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And until then, they expect me to do what, just to go fuck myself?

jokes.text: 'Sounds like Hank's fire alarm.' — Artie identifying the alarm by sound alone with total resignation
jokes.setup: A fire alarm goes off in the building
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately recognizes it as specifically Hank's alarm — as if Hank triggering fire alarms is so routine it has become identifiable to him by ear
jokes.explanation: Four words and maximum information. Artie not just identifying that Hank caused a fire but doing so instantly from the SOUND of the alarm — implying this has happened so many times Artie has developed a taxonomy of Hank-related fire alarms — is a brilliant piece of implied history. The joke rewards thinking about what it implies: how many times has this happened? Economy is near-perfect. This is the episode's most quotable single line.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Why did you give young pipsqueak yonder a fine cojiba?

jokes.text: 'This looks like Hunter Thompson's pad in the sixties.' — Artie surveying Hank's smoke-flooded, soaking-wet office
jokes.setup: Artie enters Hank's office after the sprinklers went off due to cigar smoke
jokes.punchline: Artie's cultural reference point for the disaster is Hunter S. Thompson — implying the chaos is both legendary and vaguely glamorous in a debauched way
jokes.explanation: The Hunter Thompson reference is well-matched to Artie's sensibility — he's old enough and worldly enough to invoke it naturally. The comparison between Hank's office disaster and genuine countercultural excess is funny in its disproportion: Thompson had an excuse; Hank just smoked too many cigars.

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: Look at you. You're so sexy, I'm getting a woody just looking at you.

jokes.text: 'Only you could make these goddamn sprinklers go off on some of the finest cigars in the world! You realize what a tragedy that is?'
jokes.setup: The sprinklers have destroyed Hank's premium cigars
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'tragedy' is entirely about the cigars — not the property damage, not Hank's near-accident — a perfect inversion of expected priorities
jokes.explanation: Artie's cigar devotion is so sincere that his grief for the wet Cohibas is funnier than any joke about Hank's near-death experience would be. The word 'tragedy' applied to soggy cigars is the right level of bathos.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: how can you look at yourself in the mirror in the morning?

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: It's really difficult, Larry. Because I'm not as sexy as you are.

jokes.text: Hank's account of passing out: 'between the smoke and my recent blood loss, the room just started to swim... and the sofa is on fire'
jokes.setup: Hank explains how the sprinklers got triggered
jokes.punchline: The matter-of-fact progression: smoke + 'recent blood loss' (unexplained) → room swimming → sofa on fire, delivered with Hank's characteristic self-dramatizing calm
jokes.explanation: 'My recent blood loss' as an unexplained aside is the best detail — Hank mentions it casually as if it's a known quantity, but we have no idea what happened to him, which is funnier than any explanation would be. The escalation to sofa fire is appropriately Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank. Hank gave them to me.

jokes.text: Hank's explanation: 'I think between the smoke and my recent blood loss, the room just started to swim and the next thing I know, I'm staring up at the ceiling and the sofa is on fire.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks how this happened. Hank explains his third cigar.
jokes.punchline: The casual insertion of 'my recent blood loss' with no explanation — implying a prior unreferenced injury — followed by the matter-of-fact 'the sofa is on fire.'
jokes.explanation: 'My recent blood loss' is an unexplained detail that implies an entire prior story we're not getting — the comedy is in its absolute casualness. The escalation to 'sofa is on fire' delivered as if it's just one of those things is perfectly Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Taffy.

dialogue.speaker: Inspector
dialogue.line: Taffy?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah. Yeah, I chew taffy.

jokes.text: Maintenance won't get Hank a new couch until next week — Hank: 'And until then, they expect me to do what, just to go fuck myself?'
jokes.setup: Hank's sofa burned; maintenance can't replace it for a week
jokes.punchline: Hank's rhetorical question about what he should do in the interim — expressed as profane existential despair
jokes.explanation: The phrasing of 'go fuck myself' as the only alternative to having a sofa is characteristically Hank — melodramatic, profane, and oddly specific. Gets a mild laugh from delivery rather than concept.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hot plate.

jokes.text: Hank gives Charlie — the dying child — one of his finest Cohibas as a 'memento'
jokes.setup: Hank is meeting Charlie from the One Wish Foundation; he wants to give him something memorable
jokes.punchline: Hank's gift to the sick child is a premium Cuban cigar — entirely inappropriate, but Hank delivers it with genuine warmth and the child accepts it with 'thank you, Mr. Kingsley'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. Hank gives a terminally ill child a Cuban cigar. The horror is that he does it with GENUINE warmth — 'you have very nice manners' — which makes it both funnier and slightly more disturbing. The joke also plants the seed for the payoff at episode's end (Charlie gets sick from smoking it). Everything about this moment is character-specific and earned.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Fucker.

jokes.text: Artie: 'If you're going to give him a memento, just give him a fucking white owl.'
jokes.setup: Artie is horrified that Hank gave the dying child a premium Cohiba instead of saving it
jokes.punchline: Artie's objection is not that Hank gave a child a cigar — it's that he gave him a GOOD cigar. A cheap White Owl would've been appropriate.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The comedic logic is airtight: Artie has established that he cares more about premium cigars than people; Hank giving a child one violates his hierarchy. The joke is not 'don't give cigars to sick children' — it's 'don't give GOOD cigars to sick children.' The inversion of expected moral outrage is perfectly executed. 'A fucking white owl' as the correct-grade cigar for a wish-foundation kid is both darkly specific and completely in character for Artie. Economy is nearly perfect: one line, complete devastation. This approaches the caliber of the 'snip snap' anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, fuck me.

jokes.text: Norman enters Larry's office speaking seductively: 'Hello there, Mr. Sexy... You're so sexy, I'm getting a woody just looking at you.'
jokes.setup: Norman has good news about the sexiest men alive list
jokes.punchline: Norman's delivery of the news takes the form of aggressive, performative flattery that makes Larry visibly uncomfortable — 'Don't frighten me, please'
jokes.explanation: Norman's showbiz-sycophancy dialed up to sexual absurdity is a solid character comedy beat. 'Getting a woody' from Larry's sexiness is the right level of transgressive flattery. Larry's 'don't frighten me' lands as both believable discomfort and latent vanity (he doesn't actually push back on being called sexy).

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I can't believe Hank gave you a cojiba robusto.
These rock.

jokes.text: Pause beat after Norman confirms Larry made the list — 'Thank you.' / 'You're welcome.' — then: 'Did you bump Stiller?'
jokes.setup: Larry has just learned he made the sexiest men alive list; a moment of genuine gratitude passes
jokes.punchline: Larry's first follow-up question is confirming that his friend was bumped — the warmth evaporates instantly into transactional self-interest
jokes.explanation: The economy of this beat is what elevates it. There's a pause — Larry accepts the good news with a simple 'thank you' — and then immediately: 'Did you bump Stiller?' The jump from gracious to transactional is perfectly timed and completely Larry. The callback lands harder because Ben Stiller is about to walk in. The structure rewards the audience's memory.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah? Well, thanks for ratting me out to the feds, speaking of assholes.

jokes.text: Ben Stiller arrives and Larry immediately compliments him effusively — 'You look great... you working out?' — while having just had him bumped from the list
jokes.setup: Larry just confirmed Ben Stiller was bumped from the Sexiest Men list; Ben Stiller walks in
jokes.punchline: Larry is all warmth and compliments — 'you look great,' 'your dad's great on those ESPN spots' — piling on the flattery while the audience knows he just knifed him
jokes.explanation: Dramatic irony at its most satisfying. Larry's warmth ('I'm a big fan') is grotesque given what he just did. Norman's presence in the scene adds an extra layer — he can barely contain it. The 'how can you look at yourself in the mirror in the morning?' exchange afterward (between Norman and Larry) closes the loop perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Stiller
dialogue.line: Jesus, is everybody on this show an asshole?

jokes.text: Norman to Larry after Stiller leaves: 'How can you look at yourself in the mirror in the morning?' / 'It's really difficult, Larry. Because I'm not as sexy as you are.'
jokes.setup: Larry confronted Norman with mock outrage about the ethical impossibility of what they just did
jokes.punchline: Norman deflects the moral question entirely by turning it back into flattery — using Larry's own vanity as an escape hatch — and Larry accepts this completely
jokes.explanation: Beautiful economy. Norman redirects a genuine ethical indictment into a sexiness compliment and Larry takes it. The exchange perfectly encapsulates the dynamic: Larry WANTS to be morally confronted, but his vanity will always create an off-ramp. 'Because I'm not as sexy as you are' is the exact right answer to 'how can you look in the mirror' and it shouldn't work — but it does.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey, everybody! Hey, look at Larry, the big fat asshole! Whoo! Asshole man!

jokes.text: U.S. Customs inspector arrives to question Larry about contraband Cuban cigars — Larry pivots instantly to mentioning the Secretary of Agriculture ('Nice fella. Big laugher.')
jokes.setup: A federal agent has arrived about the illegal cigars; Larry tries to manage the situation with celebrity/politician name-dropping
jokes.punchline: 'Nice fella. Big laugher.' about the Secretary of Agriculture — plus 'Too bad he's under investigation' — Larry inadvertently describing a corrupt official as though this is a networking opportunity
jokes.explanation: A perfectly observed piece of celebrity psychology. Larry's instinct when confronted by federal authority is to establish that he knows people in government — but the one he cites is under investigation. 'Big laugher' as a character reference is the right absurd detail. Larry's lack of self-awareness here is precise.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I wish you could see how Jewish you look right now.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I think, in that case, we shouldn't say another word until we have a lawyer present, right, Larry?' / Larry immediately: 'Hank. Hank gave them to me.'
jokes.setup: Artie recommends lawyering up; Larry ignores this entirely
jokes.punchline: Before Artie even finishes the sentence, Larry throws Hank under the bus — the speed of the betrayal is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top two jokes. Artie's setup ('we shouldn't say another word until') creates the expectation of restraint — and Larry immediately violates it, ratting out Hank before Artie finishes speaking. 'Hank. Hank gave them to me.' The period between the two 'Hank's is perfect — he says the name, then elaborates as if the name alone wasn't incriminating enough. Character integration is as high as it gets: only Larry's particular combination of self-preservation and obliviousness produces this. The joke is structurally flawless and rewards re-watching because of how quickly the betrayal lands.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's incredible coming from a self-hating Jew like yourself.

jokes.text: Hank denies everything: 'What cigars? I don't... I don't smoke cigars. They're filthy, disgusting. It's like putting a big turd in your mouth.'
jokes.setup: The customs agent confronts Hank about the cigars; Hank has been the episode's biggest cigar enthusiast
jokes.punchline: Hank — who has spent the entire episode doing an elaborate Spanish cigar-smuggler persona — claims to find cigars disgusting and compares them to putting 'a big turd in your mouth'
jokes.explanation: The reversal of Hank's entire episode-long character as a cigar connoisseur into sudden passionate anti-cigar sentiment is the full comedic payoff. 'Like putting a big turd in your mouth' is the right level of Hank overstatement — he doesn't just say cigars are bad, he commits to the grossest possible image.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, really? What time is the collar due back?

jokes.text: 'What do you keep in this humidor?' / 'Taffy.' / 'Taffy?' / 'Yeah. Yeah, I chew taffy. What is that? Is that a crime?'
jokes.setup: The inspector finds Hank's humidor — a device specifically designed to store cigars at proper humidity
jokes.punchline: Hank claims he uses it to store taffy — an absurd lie that he doubles down on with 'What is that? Is that a crime?' as if taffy-in-humidor is a perfectly normal arrangement
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most quotable single joke. 'Taffy' as the explanation for a humidor is perfect absurdist desperation — it's the first thing Hank's panicked brain produced and he commits to it fully. The 'Taffy?' / 'Yeah. Yeah, I chew taffy' doubled confirmation, followed by the defensive 'What is that? Is that a crime?' — the escalating indignation at an imaginary taffy crime — is masterful character comedy. Hank's commitment to the bit is both stupid and completely believable. This deserves high marks across all craft dimensions.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: you don't have to come visit me because you've already fucked me in the ass.

jokes.text: 'Well, then how do you explain the smell in this room and the fact that your couch is burned?' / 'Hot plate.'
jokes.setup: Inspector challenges Hank on the evidence of cigar use — the smell and the burned couch
jokes.punchline: 'Hot plate.' — delivered with complete brevity, as if a hot plate spontaneously burning a sofa and filling a room with premium cigar smoke is self-evident
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum comedy. The entire elaborate earlier sequence of Hank's cigar-induced inferno is reduced by Hank to 'hot plate' — a lie so minimal it barely qualifies as an explanation. Economy is literally perfect here: you cannot be more economical than two words. The gap between the evidence (sofa burned, smoke-filled humidor room) and the explanation (hot plate) is the joke. Hank's delivery would require zero elaboration — the inspector's silence is the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Charlie's sick. We got to get him to the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Who's that kid?

jokes.text: 'Fucker.' — Hank's single-word reaction to being told Larry identified him as the source
jokes.setup: The inspector tells Hank that Mr. Sanders identified him as the cigar provider
jokes.punchline: Hank says only 'Fucker.' — directed at Larry, off-camera — with complete certainty about who he means and complete resignation to the outcome
jokes.explanation: The companion joke to Larry's betrayal at 15:29. One word, perfectly placed. Hank doesn't rage, doesn't elaborate — just 'Fucker.' The period is doing heavy lifting. This is the ideal comedic reaction to learning you've been sold out: instant, resigned, specific. Character integration is near-perfect because no other character on this show could be both this wronged and this immediately resigned.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank's had a bad day.

jokes.text: The inspector allows Hank to finish the show before arresting him — 'I'll let you do the show, but immediately afterward we'll have to go downtown to process your arrest.'
jokes.setup: Hank is being formally arrested for cigar smuggling
jokes.punchline: The show takes precedence over federal law enforcement — the inspector accommodates the production schedule as a matter of professional courtesy
jokes.explanation: A great piece of showbiz absurdism — even federal arrests are subordinated to broadcast schedules. The inspector's accommodation is played completely straight, which makes it funnier. Captures the insular world of show production where the show literally always goes on.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Apparently someone let him smoke one of Hank's cigars and he got sick.

jokes.text: Tonya Bailey (People reporter) has been witnessing the entire arrest — Hank's reaction: 'Oh, fuck me.'
jokes.setup: Hank is just being arrested when he realizes the People magazine reporter has been in the room the whole time
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, fuck me.' — two words of pure resigned horror at the PR catastrophe of being caught on camera by People magazine during a customs arrest
jokes.explanation: The setup is structural (reporter has been present all episode) and the payoff is Hank's recognition of the implications. Economy is very high — the horror is proportionate and the phrasing is exactly right. The layering of the cigar storyline with the People magazine storyline pays off here.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I cannot believe you could do that to a child, Mary Lou.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Lou
dialogue.line: He wanted to, and it was really just a couple of puffs.

jokes.text: Charlie and Beverly are smoking one of Hank's cigars backstage — Beverly: 'I just have really bad allergies this time of year.'
jokes.setup: Beverly catches herself coughing on a cigar
jokes.punchline: Her explanation for the coughing — 'allergies' — transparently covering for the fact that she's smoking a contraband Cuban cigar with the dying child
jokes.explanation: The visual of Beverly smoking with Charlie (the DYING CHILD, ON OXYGEN presumably) is the comedy — the 'allergies' cover is a functional joke but not the best one in this beat. The situation sells it more than the line.

dialogue.line: Charlie has asked for a second wish.

jokes.text: 'I can't believe Hank gave you a cojiba robusto. These rock.' — Beverly, cigarette in hand, to the sick child
jokes.setup: Beverly has just lit up with Charlie; she's clearly impressed by the quality of Hank's contraband
jokes.punchline: 'These rock' — Beverly's cigar connoisseurship in this context (adult employee, dying child, illegal cigars backstage of a talk show) is the absurd culmination of the cigar subplot
jokes.explanation: Beverly's casual appreciation for the quality of illegal cigars she's sharing with a terminally ill child is a great absurdist payoff. 'These rock' in this context is the punchline to a long setup. The rewatch bonus is for how it retroactively recontextualizes Beverly's character.

jokes.text: 'Oh, I never smoked a cigar before.' / 'How old are you?' / '14.' — pause — 'You know... I was 14 when I smoked my first cigar.'
jokes.setup: Charlie admits he's never smoked a cigar; Beverly asks his age
jokes.punchline: Charlie is 14 — making Beverly's bonding memory ('I was 14 when I smoked my first cigar') entirely the wrong response to this revelation. She treats this as a charming coincidence rather than a reason to stop.
jokes.explanation: The pause between '14' and 'You know... I was 14 when I smoked my first cigar' is the structural key — it creates the expectation that Beverly will reconsider, then pivots into nostalgic bonding. The response is the wrong response at every level, which is why it's funny. Beverly has completely abandoned her professional responsibility in favor of sharing a pleasant memory with the dying child she'd been avoiding all day. Well-structured and character-revealing.

jokes.text: Ben Stiller's on-air interview: he got back in touch with his first kiss from camp, she sent a photo, 'she looked pretty good' — 'I'm considering a plane trip' — Larry: 'So it's not easy for you to get dates, huh?'
jokes.setup: Stiller is sharing a charming anecdote about reconnecting with a childhood sweetheart
jokes.punchline: Larry summarizes the entire story — which was warm and romantic — as evidence that Ben can't get dates. It's simultaneously a host non-sequitur and an accidentally devastating editorial.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Larry Sanders moment. On-air Larry is supposed to be a warm, professional interviewer — but his 'So it's not easy for you to get dates, huh?' is a complete misread that transforms Ben's sweet story into a loneliness confession. It's both a character joke (Larry as a bad listener) and a dark joke (it's kind of true about Ben's story). The cut to commercial immediately after ('Why don't we take a break?') suggests even Larry realized he crossed a line.

jokes.text: Larry's question: 'So it's not easy for you to get dates, huh?' immediately followed by commercial break cut: 'Why don't we take a break?'
jokes.setup: Stiller has rambled vulnerably about trying to reconnect with a childhood sweetheart as his romantic option.
jokes.punchline: Larry's brutal summation — 'so it's not easy for you to get dates, huh?' — cuts through the romanticism, exposing the subtext. The immediate pivot to commercial saves Stiller from having to answer.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Larry Sanders talk-show moment — the host cuts through the guest's self-presentation with brutal accuracy, then immediately hides behind the commercial break before the guest can recover. 'So it's not easy for you to get dates, huh?' is economical, accurate, and devastating. This is exactly the behavior that defines the show.

jokes.text: Larry (on air, during commercial break): 'Very funny. You look good... Have you been working out? Because, seriously, you really look like you're... pumped up. Chiseled. Really good.'
jokes.setup: They're at a commercial break; Ben Stiller is seething about the list and Larry is filling dead air with excessive compliments
jokes.punchline: Larry's escalating physical compliments ('pumped up... chiseled... really good') are hollow stalling, and both men know it — the over-the-top flattery is its own indictment
jokes.explanation: The escalating physical compliments ('pumped up... chiseled... really good') work as cringe comedy because we know what's about to happen — Stiller is about to confront Larry — and Larry's oblivious flattery makes the impending scene funnier. The 'how's that low-fat...' abandoned question suggests even Larry knows this isn't working.

jokes.text: Ben Stiller: 'Shut up, all right? I know you had me bumped from the list.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been complimenting Ben during the commercial break; Ben cuts through it
jokes.punchline: Ben knows. The compliments are exposed as guilt management, and 'shut up' is the perfect syllable to end them.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the entire Stiller subplot. 'Shut up, all right?' is the right register — not explosive anger but exhausted contempt. The structure of the subplot (setup → bump → flattery → exposure) is well-executed across 15 minutes of episode time.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Where did you hear that?' — Hank walks in immediately: 'You're an asshole, Hank.' / 'Yeah? Well, thanks for ratting me out to the feds, speaking of assholes.' / 'Jesus, is everybody on this show an asshole?'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to deny the Stiller bump; Hank enters having just been arrested
jokes.punchline: Within seconds, three men are calling each other assholes — Hank arriving to counter-betray, culminating in Stiller's meta-observation that the show seems to be staffed entirely by assholes
jokes.explanation: The three-way escalation of mutual betrayal accusations is well-choreographed. Ben Stiller's 'Jesus, is everybody on this show an asshole?' works as a meta-observation — he's essentially reviewing the show he's guesting on. The convergence of both subplots in one room is satisfying structurally.

jokes.text: Hank is in the audience, drunkenly yelling 'Hey, look at Larry, the big fat asshole! Asshole man!' to the live studio audience
jokes.setup: Hank has stormed out of the confrontation and apparently gone to the audience floor
jokes.punchline: Hank grandstanding to the live studio audience — 'Asshole man!' — like a drunk at a sports event, while they're still mid-commercial break
jokes.explanation: Hank addressing the studio audience as if they are at a sporting event to denounce Larry is a great escalation of Hank's meltdown. 'Asshole man!' is inspired — it's not even a coherent insult, just Hank at maximum grievance. The idea of the live audience witnessing this during a commercial break is a sharp piece of show-within-a-show comedy.

jokes.text: Hank tells Larry: 'You know, I heard the car show is in town next week. Maybe if you suck off Lee Iacocca, he'll give you miss auto parts.'
jokes.setup: Hank is furious at being betrayed by Larry on the sexiest men list — he's now fighting back
jokes.punchline: Hank suggests Larry perform a sex act on Lee Iacocca (elderly Chrysler CEO) to win a car-related beauty title — a grotesque image designed to insult Larry's masculinity and the pettiness of his vanity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Lee Iacocca — not a random executive but a specific 70s-era celebrity CEO — and 'miss auto parts' as the prize make this more than a generic insult. Hank's revenge fantasies always involve elaborate humiliation. The joke is Hank-specific in its theatrical excess.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I wish you could see how Jewish you look right now.' / Hank: 'That's incredible coming from a self-hating Jew like yourself.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Hank are in a full backstage screaming match while Ben Stiller watches
jokes.punchline: The argument devolves into competing accusations of Jewish neurosis — Larry using it as a physical insult, Hank weaponizing 'self-hating Jew' as the counter — both accusations carrying truth
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific. This exchange works on multiple levels: (1) it's accurate about both characters, (2) Garry Shandling and Jeffrey Tambor are Jewish, which makes it meta, (3) 'how Jewish you look right now' as the specific insult is unexpected and original. The counter — 'self-hating Jew like yourself' — is both a comedy comeback and a genuine character indictment of Larry. This is the kind of joke that only works in a show this specific about its characters.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Listen, I just want you to know that if I go to prison, you don't have to come visit me because you've already fucked me in the ass.'
jokes.setup: Hank is facing arrest thanks to Larry's immediate betrayal to the customs inspector
jokes.punchline: Hank refuses prison visits because the metaphorical violation has already occurred
jokes.explanation: Good dark callback — the prison visit concept (usually a gesture of loyalty) is reframed through Hank's betrayal wound. The vulgarity is precise rather than gratuitous: it's both literal (he's going to prison) and metaphorical (Larry betrayed him). The construction 'you don't have to come visit me BECAUSE you've already...' is a clean inversion. Quotable.

jokes.text: 'Oh, really? What time is the collar due back?' — Hank to Larry, implying Larry is a dog on a leash
jokes.setup: The argument continues; Hank appears to glance at something — possibly a costume or clothing piece — and deploys a non-sequitur insult
jokes.punchline: 'What time is the collar due back?' — implying Larry is someone else's pet, possibly referencing his relationship with the network or a girlfriend controlling him
jokes.explanation: A sharp insult that lands because it's indirect and visual — Hank appears to be looking at something on Larry (possibly an accessory) and uses it to imply subservience. The 'collar' metaphor has multiple possible readings that all work against Larry.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Listen, I just want you to know that if I go to prison, you don't have to come visit me because you've already fucked me in the ass.'
jokes.setup: Hank is facing a federal arrest; he addresses Larry with final words
jokes.punchline: The prison rape metaphor applied to the list betrayal — 'you've already fucked me in the ass' — as a literal prison consequence and figurative description of what Larry did
jokes.explanation: The double meaning — prison sexual violence as metaphor for the betrayal, with the implication that going to prison would only extend the violation — is darker than most of the episode's comedy. The structure is clean: setup (if I go to prison), misdirect (you don't have to visit), punchline (you've already done the bad thing). Hank's wounded dignity is perfectly captured.

jokes.text: Artie's interruption of the fight: 'What the hell is going on? Sounds like a fucking hockey game!'
jokes.setup: A three-way backstage fight is raging with multiple insults flying.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'hockey game' comparison — not a brawl, not a riot, specifically a hockey game — is an unexpected specificity.
jokes.explanation: A solid Artie interruption. 'Fucking hockey game' is a good specific simile — hockey implies organized but violent and chaotic. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Charlie collapsing/getting sick backstage — Artie: 'Who's that kid?' / Random staffer: 'That's the kid from the one wish foundation.' / Artie: 'OK, gentlemen, we've got to do this show for Charlie.'
jokes.setup: The backstage meltdown between Larry, Hank, and Stiller is at peak intensity
jokes.punchline: Charlie's medical emergency is what finally stops the fight — but Artie immediately transforms it into motivation for the show ('we've got to do this show for Charlie'), a parody of sports-movie rallying cries
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most structurally satisfying jokes. The child who was being avoided all day — whose illness caused anxiety and required an elaborate stalling operation — now becomes the rallying cry for the show. Artie's transformation of a medical emergency into a pep talk ('we've got to do this show FOR Charlie') is simultaneously cynical and genuinely unaware, which is the Artie sweet spot. The fact that Artie needed to be told who the kid is ('who's that kid?') caps it perfectly.

jokes.text: Charlie being rushed to the hospital stops the fight: 'Charlie's sick. We got to get him to the hospital.' — then Hank asks: 'Who's that kid?'
jokes.setup: The backstage fight is interrupted by an emergency — the One Wish Foundation child is sick.
jokes.punchline: Hank, who met Charlie, gave him a cigar, and addressed him warmly, immediately asks 'Who's that kid?' — having entirely forgotten him.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly dark Hank moment — he bonded with this child and gave him a cigar earlier in the episode, and now he has absolutely no memory of him. 'Who's that kid?' is an economical character encapsulation.

jokes.text: Larry on air: 'I just want to say to a special friend of ours, Charlie, who should be watching the show tonight... we're with you, buddy.' / Ben Stiller: 'I don't know you and I never really talked to you, but I heard a lot about you... hang in there, buddy.'
jokes.setup: Larry makes a heartfelt public shout-out to Charlie
jokes.punchline: Ben Stiller's contribution — 'I don't know you and I never really talked to you, but I heard a lot about you' — is the most honest (and therefore funniest) tribute possible: completely hollow, delivered as warmth
jokes.explanation: Stiller's on-air tribute is accidentally the most devastating indictment of the entire episode's premise: the kid's wish was to meet Larry, they spent the day avoiding him, and the public tribute from a celebrity guest is 'I don't know you and I never talked to you.' The honesty is the joke. This is the show's satirical thesis delivered through accidental sincerity.

jokes.text: Ben Stiller on air, addressing Charlie: 'I don't know you and I never really talked to you, but I heard a lot about you. I feel like I know you, so just... hang in there, buddy.'
jokes.setup: The show returns from the backstage chaos; Larry and Stiller are asked to address Charlie in a sincere moment.
jokes.punchline: Stiller's message to a dying child he has literally never met is to confirm that he has not met him, then offer 'hang in there, buddy' — the most generic possible sympathy.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully observed celebrity-performing-sincerity comedy — Stiller's message is technically honest ('I don't know you and never really talked to you') while being a perfect example of performative empathy from someone with no actual connection. 'Hang in there, buddy' as the destination is perfect.

jokes.text: Hank is asked to say something to Charlie on air — says nothing. Larry: 'Hank's had a bad day.'
jokes.setup: Larry invites Hank to address Charlie; Hank is sitting there facing a federal arrest
jokes.punchline: Hank says nothing. Larry covers: 'Hank's had a bad day.' — perhaps the most technically accurate understatement of the episode
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and a strong contender for the highest scores. Every element is perfect: Hank has been arrested, betrayed, humiliated, lost his sofa, given a dying child a cigar, been publicly exposed in People magazine — and Larry summarizes all of this on national television as 'Hank's had a bad day.' The understatement is so total it becomes a kind of poetry. It's a callback to everything in the episode simultaneously. It's live on air. And it's delivered with Larry's trademark breezy obliviousness. This is what 9+ looks like: it earns its score through perfect structure, character integration, and economy simultaneously.

jokes.text: Post-show: Artie learns Charlie got sick because 'someone let him smoke one of Hank's cigars' — and it was 'only a couple of puffs'
jokes.setup: Artie is relieved that Charlie is going to be fine
jokes.punchline: Charlie didn't have a medical episode from his illness — he got sick from smoking Hank's illegal Cuban cigar at age 14. The cigar subplot and the sick-kid subplot converge in the worst possible way.
jokes.explanation: The narrative payoff of the episode's two main subplots colliding. The kid who is terminally ill got hospitalized not by his condition but by Hank's contraband cigar — which Beverly was also smoking with him. The moral inversion is complete: everyone was so worried about Larry's emotional fragility that they accidentally made the sick child sicker. 'It was only a couple of puffs' is the right minimizing defense. This is a well-structured episode-length joke.

jokes.text: Artie lectures Beverly and Mary Lou for letting Charlie smoke — then: 'Ladies, please, you are ruining my post-show high!'
jokes.setup: Artie is appropriately horrified that they let a child smoke a cigar
jokes.punchline: Mid-lecture, Artie breaks to prioritize his own post-show mood — 'you are ruining my post-show high' — revealing that his cigars are now being smoked too
jokes.explanation: Artie's interruption of his own moral lecture to complain about his mood is a perfectly Artie joke. It reveals that he's also smoking post-show — probably the wet Cohibas he 'got rid of' for Hank. 'Post-show high' is a great phrase. The self-interruption structure is economical and character-true.

jokes.text: 'The important thing is that Charlie had a good time. He's a great kid. At least we were able to make him happy for one day.'
jokes.setup: The episode is wrapping up; Beverly offers a feel-good summary
jokes.punchline: Beverly's wholesome reflection — 'we made him happy for one day' — glosses over the fact that they avoided him for most of the day, accidentally gave him a cigar, and sent him to the hospital
jokes.explanation: A solid ironic button on the wish-foundation subplot. Beverly's revisionist warmth is standard sitcom coda — but here the gap between 'we made him happy' and what actually happened is the comedy. Works better in context than as a standalone quote.

jokes.text: 'Charlie has asked for a second wish.' — final line of the episode
jokes.setup: Beverly has just concluded that they gave Charlie a great day; the episode is ostensibly wrapping with warm feelings
jokes.punchline: Charlie has already used his one wish and is asking for another — implying the day was such a disaster that it didn't count, OR that the kid liked it so much he wants another, which given the cigar hospitalization is equally horrifying
jokes.explanation: The episode's perfect closing joke. 'Charlie has asked for a second wish' is an episode-length callback that works on multiple interpretations simultaneously: (1) The visit was so bad that his wish effectively wasn't granted and he needs a redo. (2) He had such a weirdly good time that he wants more. (3) The wish foundation apparently has sequel wishes. The ambiguity is the genius — you can't tell if Charlie is complaining or enthusiastic. The cold ending on this line, with no resolution, is exactly right for Larry Sanders' tone. Structure-wise, it's a perfect button on everything that came before.

tmdb_overview: Larry wants to be on People's Ten Sexiest Men list, even if it means bumping off guest Ben Stiller. Beverly gets stuck taking care of their ""One Wish"" Foundation child when he comes to meet Larry. Hank distributes his illegally obtained Cuban cigars.
